newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany does plan to sell Bundesbank gold - Stern.
newsitem.headline: Germany does plan to sell Bundesbank gold - Stern.

text.p: The German government, despite official denials, is planning to sell part of the Bundesbank's gold and foreign reserves after the startup of the European Central Bank, the weekly Stern reported on Tuesday.

In advance excerpts from its Thursday edition, Stern said, without citing sources, that some elements of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition hoped to start such sales in July 1998 to reduce Germany's outstanding debt.
Government officials were not immediately available for comment on the Stern report.

In the current spat between Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, Waigel has repeatedly said the central bank's reserves would merely be revalued to current market prices.
Kohl also said on Monday that "not a single gram of gold and not a single dollar" would be sold.
Waigel hopes the extraordinary profit from the revaluation would help Germany meet the requirements for European monetary union (EMU).

The European Central Bank, which will assume the powers of all of Europe's central banks, will be capitalised at the equivalent of 95 billion marks, of which Germany will have to put up 24 billion marks, Stern said.
But that will leave the lion's share of the Bundesbank's reserves -- which Stern says are worth 150 billion marks at current market values -- lying idle in the Bundesbank's vaults.

Stern said Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg, the designated president of the ECB, has criticised plans to transfer extraordinary profits from the revaluation of Bundesbank assets to the German government.
Duisenberg told a group of four German parliamentarians that the plan runs counter to the principles of steady and solid budget policy.
